title: Audit Reporting, Corrective Action, and Follow-Up
learningObjectives: Write a clear, actionable audit report that drives improvement
Evaluate root cause analyses submitted by auditees in response to nonconformities
Assess whether proposed corrective actions are adequate to prevent recurrence
Manage the audit follow-up process and close nonconformities effectively

content.text: The Audit Report: Structure and Purpose

The audit report is the primary output of the audit. It must be accurate, clear, concise, and based entirely on objective evidence. Its purpose is to communicate the audit findings to management in a way that drives effective corrective action and continual improvement — not to create a legal document or assign blame.

items: Executive Summary: overall audit conclusion, summary of findings, certification recommendation (for third-party audits)
Audit Details: objectives, scope, criteria, dates, locations, audit team, auditee representatives
Audit Findings Summary: table listing all nonconformities (major and minor) with clause references
Detailed Findings: for each NC — the requirement, the evidence, the gap, and the classification
Positive Observations: noteworthy good practices that should be recognised and maintained
Opportunities for Improvement: observations that are not NCs but represent good improvement opportunities
Audit Conclusion: statement of overall conformance and system effectiveness

content.text: Audit reports must be factual and evidence-based. Every nonconformity statement must cite specific objective evidence — records, dates, interview quotes, observations. Subjective opinions ('the safety culture seems poor') are not appropriate in a formal audit report. If you observed specific behaviours that concern you, describe exactly what you observed.

rows: ISO 45001:2018 Clause 7.2 requires the organisation to ensure workers are competent based on education, training, or experience

Of the 12 worker training records reviewed, 5 contained no evidence of competence evaluation after initial training. The records for J. Smith (Maintenance Tech), R. Ali (Process Operator), and 3 others showed training completion dates of 2021 with no subsequent assessment.

The documented procedure (HSE-TRN-002 Rev 4, Section 4.3) requires annual competence verification for all workers in safety-critical roles. No competence evaluations have been recorded for these workers in 2022 or 2023.

content.text: After receiving the audit report, the auditee must provide a corrective action response for each nonconformity. A good corrective action response has three mandatory elements: (1) Root cause analysis — why did the NC occur, not just what happened; (2) Corrective action — what will be changed to address the root cause; (3) Completion date — a realistic, committed date.

The process of identifying the underlying cause(s) of a nonconformity or problem, rather than just the immediate cause. Common methods: 5 Whys, fishbone (Ishikawa) diagram, fault tree analysis. The root cause is the point at which intervention would prevent recurrence.

NC: Workers in the confined space entry programme have not been re-certified in over 18 months (required every 12 months). Immediate cause: training was not scheduled. Root cause (5 Whys): Why not scheduled? No reminder system existed. Why no reminder? The training calendar was a paper system updated manually. Why paper? No one was assigned to maintain an automated system. Why not assigned? No defined role in the OHSMS for training programme administration. Root cause: organisational gap — no defined responsibility for training programme maintenance. Corrective action: assign training programme administration to a named role; implement electronic training tracking system with automated reminders; conduct a full compliance review of all certification currencies.

The auditor must review corrective action responses and judge whether they are adequate — specifically: does the proposed action address the root cause, not just the symptom? A corrective action that only fixes the specific instances found (re-trains the five workers with lapsed records) without addressing the systemic cause (no reminder system) will not prevent recurrence and is therefore inadequate.

items: Adequate: changes the process, procedure, system, or responsibility that caused the NC
Inadequate: only addresses the specific instance found without preventing recurrence
Inadequate: commits to future actions without changing the underlying system
Inadequate: root cause analysis stops at 'human error' without exploring why the error was possible

content.text: Audit nonconformities are not closed by the auditee's corrective action plan — they are closed by the auditor's verification that the corrective action was implemented and effective. For minor NCs, this may be a document review. For major NCs, re-audit may be required. Surveillance audits provide ongoing verification.

The audit programme manager must periodically evaluate whether the audit programme is effective: Are audits finding real issues or rubber-stamping? Are NC trends improving? Are corrective actions sustainable? Are audit findings being used to drive management review inputs? A healthy programme shows a genuine mix of conformities, observations, and nonconformities — an audit that finds nothing is usually a sign of an ineffective audit, not a perfect system.

Gulf Context: Follow-up on audit nonconformities is an area where Gulf HSE management systems often need strengthening. On large projects with many contractors, corrective action tracking becomes extremely complex — hundreds of NCs across dozens of contractors must be tracked to closure. Gulf operators use contractor HSE performance management systems (SAMS in Aramco, HSEMS portal in ADNOC) to track NC status in real time. A Gulf HSE professional who can manage a large audit programme — plan audits, train internal auditors, track NCs, verify corrective actions, and present programme performance to management — is extremely valuable. The IRCA Certified ISO 45001 Lead Auditor qualification, combined with Gulf operational experience, is one of the most sought-after credential combinations for senior Gulf HSE roles.
